title: Works of mercy for the soul
word: Works of mercy for the soul
hook: teach, counsel, correct gently, comfort, forgive, bear wrongs, pray

segments.voice: Yesterday, works of mercy for the body: Tobit's burial, and the least of these. Your line was mercy with hands. Which one did you do? Day one thousand two hundred nine.

Job has lost nearly everything: his children, his wealth, his health. He sits in the ashes. Three friends hear about it and travel to see him, and when they arrive they barely recognize him. They weep, they tear their robes, and then they do something remarkable. In the King James words: "they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." A week of silence, side by side in the dirt. It may be the best thing they ever did for him. Because then the talking started. Today: works of mercy for the soul.

Yesterday's list was for the body. Christian tradition keeps a second list, for the heart and the mind, and each item on it is something done with words, or with the holding back of words. Teach someone who doesn't know. Counsel someone who doubts. Correct someone gently. Comfort the sorrowful. Forgive. Bear wrongs patiently. Pray for others. Each one has roots in scripture. Correcting, for instance, comes with a warning label. Paul writes, "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." Restore, not crush. And remember you could be next. Comfort, in Paul, travels in a circle: God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble." Comfort received becomes comfort passed on. Now back to Job. After the week of silence, Job speaks first, cursing the day he was born. Then his friends answer, and for chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him. You must have done something. Confess it. God is punishing you. They meant to counsel and correct. But at the end of the book God says to one of them, "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." That's the warning built into these works. Words can heal or wound, and the same sentence can do either. The friends were best when they were silent and present. So the tradition pairs these works with patience and humility. On the last item, churches differ: Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the living and the dead; Protestant churches have taught differently about prayer for the dead, and differ among themselves. Prayer for the living is shared.

Here's the practice: choose one word of mercy. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself the list as questions. Is there someone who needs to learn something you know? Someone doubting? Someone you need to correct, gently? Someone grieving? Someone to forgive? A wrong you could carry quietly? Someone to pray for? Let one rise to the top. Then, before deciding what to say, sit with that person in your mind for a while in silence, the way Job's friends did at first. If you pray, you can pray for them now. The bell holds the time.
Works of mercy for the soul. Teach, counsel, correct gently, comfort, forgive, bear wrongs, and pray for others.

howItsDone: Christians practice the works of mercy for the soul, often called the spiritual works of mercy, through teaching, counseling, comforting the grieving, forgiving and praying for others; Catholic and Orthodox Christians include prayer for the dead.

Prayer for the dead: Catholic and Orthodox practice; 'many Protestants pray for the living only'. Some Anglicans and Lutherans also pray for the dead. Confirm wording.
